meta.title: Septic Shock: Neonatal & Pediatric
meta.subtitle: Recognition, Risk Stratification & Management
guideline_sources: ACCM/PALS 2017 (Davis et al., Crit Care Med)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign Pediatric 2020 (Weiss et al., PCCM)
meta.scope: Level I / Level II / Level II+ Nursery | Rural Emergency Department

popup.protocols: Suspect sepsis/shock when ANY of the following are present: (1) Tachycardia for age, (2) Temperature instability, (3) Altered mental status, (4) Prolonged capillary refill >3 sec, (5) Mottling or pallor, (6) Increased work of breathing or apnea, (7) Petechiae/purpura. In neonates: hypotension is a LATE sign — do NOT wait for low BP.
popup.evidence: Phoenix Criteria 2024 (JAMA 331:665): pediatric sepsis defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction from dysregulated host response to infection. PMID: 38245560. Hypotension is late in pediatrics — treat clinical shock before BP falls.
popup.alerts: ACTIVATE RESPONSE TEAM. Assign roles. Start timer. Two-provider minimum.

popup.protocols: Age determines organism probability, fluid volume safety, vital sign thresholds, antibiotic choice, and vasopressor dosing. Always verify gestational age for neonates — preterm physiology differs critically from term.
popup.evidence: Wynn & Wong, Clin Perinatol 2010 (PMID: 20569814): neonatal septic shock physiology differs fundamentally from older children and adults. ACCM guidelines are age-stratified.
popup.alerts: For preterm neonates: LOWER fluid volumes, EARLIER vasopressors, HIGHER IVH risk.

popup.protocols: Neonates require age-specific management. Identify: (1) EOS (<72h) vs LOS (≥72h), (2) Gestational age (term ≥37w vs preterm), (3) Maternal risk factors (GBS status, PPROM, chorioamnionitis, fever), (4) Prior antibiotic exposure (NICU/HAI risk). These four factors drive organism prediction and antibiotic selection.
popup.dosing: Normal neonatal BP: MAP ≥ gestational age (weeks) in mmHg. Term: SBP 60–90 mmHg. Preterm 28–32w: SBP 40–60 mmHg.
popup.evidence: StatPearls: Neonatal Sepsis, NBK531478 (updated Jan 2026). EOS attack rate <1% to >35% depending on GA. LOS accounts for majority of NICU sepsis deaths.
popup.alerts: Neonates present with COLD SHOCK (low CO, high SVR). Warm shock is uncommon. Do NOT assume distributive physiology.

popup.protocols: EOS = < 72 hours of life. LOS = ≥ 72 hours. Some definitions extend EOS to 7 days for term infants. EOS is predominantly maternally-transmitted. LOS is predominantly nosocomial or environmental.
popup.evidence: StatPearls NBK531478. EOS organisms: GBS, E. coli, Listeria. LOS organisms: CoNS, S. aureus (MRSA), Klebsiella, Pseudomonas (NICU).
popup.alerts: GBS EOS can present as fulminant respiratory failure within hours. Listeria EOS can present with skin lesions and meconium-stained fluid.

popup.protocols: EOS Risk Factors: GBS colonization (inadequate or no prophylaxis), PPROM >18h, maternal fever ≥38°C, chorioamnionitis, prematurity <37w. Maternal GBS prophylaxis requires penicillin (or alternatives) given ≥4h before delivery for adequate coverage.
popup.dosing: Empiric: Ampicillin 50–100 mg/kg IV q8–12h (age-based) + Gentamicin 4–5 mg/kg IV q24–48h (extended interval). Add cefotaxime 50 mg/kg q6–8h if meningitis suspected. Add acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV encephalitis possible.
popup.evidence: AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases. ACOG + AAP GBS Management Guidelines 2020. Ampicillin+gentamicin covers >99% of EOS organisms in the USA.
popup.alerts: Listeria: requires AMPICILLIN — NOT cephalosporins. Ceftriaxone has NO Listeria coverage. Do NOT substitute.

popup.protocols: Assess ALL of the following: HR, CRT, skin color, mental status, respiratory status, glucose. Obtain: iStat/IRMA blood gas (pH, BD, lactate) and point-of-care glucose immediately. Wynn-Wong Neonatal Septic Shock definition requires cardiovascular dysfunction: need for fluid/vasopressor support OR 2 of (BD >5, lactate >2× ULN, UO <0.5 mL/kg/h, CRT >5 sec).
popup.dosing: Lactate >4 mmol/L = critical. BD < –10 = severe. AG = Na – (Cl + HCO3); normal 8–12.
popup.evidence: Gago et al., J Neonatol Clin Pediatr 2022: BD >5 and elevated lactate define neonatal cardiovascular dysfunction for septic shock.
popup.alerts: ALWAYS check glucose immediately. Neonates have minimal glycogen reserve. Treat <50 mg/dL with D10W 2 mL/kg IV push.

children.label: Compensated Shock
children.sublabel: Tachycardia ± mild signs, BD 0 to –5, Lactate 2–4

popup.protocols: 1. Establish IV/IO access. 2. Blood culture × 1 set. 3. Labs: iStat pH/BD/lactate, glucose, CBC, CMP. 4. Ampicillin + Gentamicin IV STAT. 5. NS 10 mL/kg over 30 min. 6. Reassess HR, CRT after bolus. 7. Glucose: treat if <50 mg/dL with D10W 2 mL/kg. 8. ACTIVATE TRANSPORT.
popup.dosing: Fluid: NS 10 mL/kg over 30 min. Glucose: D10W 2 mL/kg IV push if <50 mg/dL, then D10W continuous infusion at maintenance. Ampicillin: 50–100 mg/kg IV. Gentamicin: 4–5 mg/kg IV q24–48h.
popup.evidence: ACCM 2017: initial 10–20 mL/kg crystalloid with reassessment. SSC Pediatric 2020: balanced crystalloids preferred over NS for volumes >20 mL/kg. PMID: 32032273.
popup.alerts: Serial lactate every 60–90 min. If lactate worsening or not clearing >10–20% per 2h — escalate to uncompensated protocol.

popup.protocols: SIMULTANEOUS ACTIONS: (1) IV/IO access — if no IV in 90 sec → IO NOW. (2) Airway: consider PPV/intubation if apnea or severe distress. (3) Blood culture × 1, then antibiotics IMMEDIATELY. (4) NS 10 mL/kg over 15 min — repeat × 1 if term infant (max 20 mL/kg total in preterm). (5) If no improvement → DOPAMINE. (6) Glucose every 30 min. (7) FFP if DIC. (8) TRANSPORT TEAM CALLED.
popup.dosing: Dopamine: start 5–10 mcg/kg/min; titrate by 2–3 mcg q10–20 min to max 20. Epinephrine alternative: 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min (NOT first-line solo agent). Hydrocortisone adjuvant: 1–2 mg/kg IV q6–8h for pressor-dependent shock. D10W: 2 mL/kg IV push, then infusion. FFP: 10–15 mL/kg if DIC (Plt <50k, prolonged PT/PTT).
popup.evidence: Foote et al., J Perinatol 2023 (PMID 37055478): dopamine used in 92% of NICU septic shock episodes. Hydrocortisone adjuvant associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.60). Epinephrine alone: higher mortality (aOR 4.7).
popup.alerts: PRETERM < 30 WEEKS: MAX 10 mL/kg × 1 bolus, then vasopressors. Rapid/large volume → IVH risk. Check ionized calcium — hypocalcemia depresses myocardial contractility. Treat iCa <1.0 mmol/L with CaGluconate 100–200 mg/kg IV over 30 min.

popup.protocols: LOS Assessment: (1) Is there a central line (PICC, UVC, UAC)? If yes — line is presumptive source. Discuss removal with receiving team. (2) NICU patient vs community? NICU → MRSA/CoNS/resistant GNB risk. Community → GBS, S. aureus, E. coli. (3) Any skin/soft tissue source? (4) NEC? Abdominal distension + bloody stool → NEC rule-out immediately.
popup.dosing: Community LOS: Ampicillin + Gentamicin (if GBS/E.coli risk) OR Vancomycin + Gentamicin (if MRSA risk). NICU/HAI LOS: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg q6–8h + Gentamicin 4–5 mg/kg q24–48h. If Pseudomonas risk: + Piperacillin-Tazobactam 75–100 mg/kg q6–8h.
popup.evidence: Glaser et al., Neoreviews 2022 (PMC9675597): CoNS most common LOS pathogen. Gram-negative LOS accounts for 70% of fatal neonatal septic shock cases (Gago 2022).
popup.alerts: MRSA LOS: remove central line as source control. Vancomycin AUC/MIC monitoring preferred. NEVER use cephalosporins as MRSA monotherapy.

popup.protocols: Gram-NEGATIVE pattern: explosive onset, severe DIC (platelets crashing), lactate >4, WBC very low (leukopenia = ominous), PCT >10 ng/mL, NEC association. Gram-POSITIVE pattern: more insidious onset, myocardial depression (cardiac function), moderate thrombocytopenia, usually leukocytosis, CoNS = indolent; MRSA = aggressive with toxin-mediated effects.
popup.evidence: Gago et al. 2022: gram-negative organisms = 90% of fatal LOS cases. Analysis of blood indicators in neonatal sepsis with different pathogenic bacteria (PMC12240254 2025): CRP, PCT, platelets are independent discriminators between gram-negative and gram-positive neonatal sepsis.
popup.alerts: You cannot determine gram stain before culture results — empiric coverage must cover BOTH pending results. The clinical pattern guides suspicion but does not confirm.

children.label: GNB-Pattern LOS
children.sublabel: Low platelets, DIC, lactate >4, PCT >10, leukopenia

popup.protocols: CRITICAL GNB PROTOCOL: (1) Immediate IO/IV. (2) Blood culture × 1. (3) Vancomycin + Gentamicin STAT. If Pseudomonas suspected: + Pip-Tazo. (4) NS 10 mL/kg (preterm) or 20 mL/kg (term) over 15–30 min. (5) Dopamine 5–10 mcg/kg/min if fluid-refractory. (6) FFP 10–15 mL/kg for DIC. (7) NEC workup: abdominal XR, surgical consult if pneumoperitoneum. (8) Line removal discussion with NICU.
popup.dosing: Vancomycin: 15–20 mg/kg IV q6–8h. Gentamicin: 4–5 mg/kg IV q24–48h. Pip-Tazo: 75–100 mg/kg q6h. Dopamine: 5–20 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone adjuvant: 1–2 mg/kg q6–8h. FFP: 10–15 mL/kg. Platelets: 10–20 mL/kg if <50,000 with bleeding.
popup.evidence: Kharrat & Jain, Pediatr Res 2022 (PMID: 33986552): gram-negative LOS produces most severe hemodynamic dysfunction via endotoxin-mediated NOS activation. Foote 2023: hydrocortisone aOR 0.60 for mortality.
popup.alerts: GNB LOS mortality peaks at 71% in ELBW (<1000g) infants (Wynn & Wong). TRANSPORT NOW. Do not wait for culture results to escalate care.

popup.protocols: GPB LOS PROTOCOL: (1) Establish IV access (line removal may be needed). (2) Blood culture × 1. (3) Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q6–8h STAT. (4) NS 10–20 mL/kg over 30 min — reassess. (5) If CVC present: notify receiving NICU for removal decision. (6) Echocardiography consideration: S. aureus LOS — rule out endocarditis and septic emboli. (7) Dopamine if fluid-refractory.
popup.dosing: Vancomycin: 15–20 mg/kg IV q6–8h (goal AUC/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L). Gentamicin: add if Enterococcus suspected. Dopamine: 5–10 mcg/kg/min if needed. Duration: S. aureus bacteremia → minimum 14 days IV antibiotics (longer if endocarditis).
popup.evidence: Glaser et al., Neoreviews 2022: CoNS LOS = most common NICU pathogen. MRSA LOS associated with higher mortality than MSSA. Functional echo (TnECHO) emerging tool for neonatal septic shock hemodynamic phenotyping (Gunjan et al., Eur J Pediatr 2024, PMID: 38276999).
popup.alerts: S. aureus LOS: always consider endocarditis (right-sided = pulmonary septic emboli). Line removal is critical source control. CoNS may be contaminant if only 1 of 2 cultures positive — clinical correlation required.

popup.protocols: Pediatric septic shock requires age-stratified vital sign assessment. Key differences from neonates: (1) More common warm/distributive shock pattern. (2) Better cardiac reserve allows longer compensation. (3) Hypotension still a late sign. (4) Community-acquired infections dominate (vs. nosocomial in neonates). Assess: level of consciousness, CRT, skin perfusion, HR/RR/BP for age.
popup.dosing: Age-appropriate tachycardia thresholds: 1–12 mo >180; 1–5y >140; 6–12y >130; >12y >110. Hypotension: 1–12 mo <70; 1–5y <70+(2×age); 6–12y <90; >12y <90 mmHg systolic.
popup.evidence: Weiss & Fitzgerald, Pediatrics Jan 2024 (PMID 38086829): updated sepsis management sub-phenotypes. SSC Pediatric 2020 PMID 32032273. Cruz et al., J ACEP Open 2020.
popup.alerts: In children, by the time they are hypotensive they have lost >25–35% of effective circulating volume. TREAT BEFORE HYPOTENSION.

popup.protocols: Age determines empiric antibiotic choice: 1–3 months: still consider GBS/Listeria + add S. pneumoniae, E. coli. 3 months–12 years: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, S. aureus, E. coli. Adolescent: N. meningitidis, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, enteric GNB.
popup.evidence: StatPearls Shock NBK531492. Medscape pediatric septic shock guidelines.
popup.alerts: Any age with petechiae/purpura + fever = meningococcemia until proven otherwise. GIVE CEFTRIAXONE IMMEDIATELY.

popup.protocols: 1–3 month infants still at risk for neonatal organisms (GBS, E. coli) PLUS community-acquired pathogens (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis). Always include meningitis coverage. Lumbar puncture should be attempted if stable, but do NOT delay antibiotics for LP.
popup.dosing: Empiric: Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q6h + Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV q6–8h. Alternative: Ampicillin + Gentamicin if cephalosporin shortage. Fluid: 10–20 mL/kg NS or LR over 15–30 min. Up to 40–60 mL/kg total in first hour. Vasopressor: dopamine or epinephrine if fluid-refractory.
popup.evidence: ACCM 2017 age-stratified guidelines. Cefotaxime preferred over ceftriaxone <1 month (biliary sludge risk), acceptable 1–3 months.
popup.alerts: If LP delayed — still give antibiotics. Sterile meningitis CSF can be obtained later. Withholding antibiotics for LP is never appropriate in an unstable infant.

popup.protocols: Assess: HR, BP, CRT, mental status, SpO2, lactate. Septic shock = inadequate tissue perfusion requiring vasopressor support OR lactate >2 mmol/L. In infants, tachycardia >180 + CRT >3 sec + altered feeding/responsiveness = shock even with normal BP.
popup.evidence: Phoenix Criteria 2024, JAMA. Children with septic shock and lactate >4 mmol/L: 22× higher mortality vs lactate <1 (pediatric ROC analysis).
popup.alerts: Check glucose NOW. Infants have limited glycogen stores. Hypoglycemia (<60 mg/dL) worsens neurologic outcomes.

popup.protocols: Golden Hour Bundle: (1) IV access × 2. (2) Blood cultures × 1 set. (3) Ampicillin + Cefotaxime IV STAT. (4) NS 20 mL/kg over 20–30 min. (5) Reassess: HR, CRT, mental status, glucose. (6) Repeat lactate in 90 min. (7) ACTIVATE TRANSPORT.
popup.dosing: Ampicillin: 50 mg/kg IV q6h. Cefotaxime: 50 mg/kg IV q6–8h. Fluids: 20 mL/kg NS or LR. D10W 2 mL/kg if glucose <60 mg/dL.
popup.evidence: ACCM 2017 first-hour bundle: fluid + antibiotics + vasopressors as needed within 60 min associated with improved survival.
popup.alerts: Serial monitoring: repeat iStat at 60–90 min. If lactate not clearing by >10–20% → escalate to vasopressor protocol.

popup.protocols: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: (1) IV/IO access — IO if no IV in 90 sec. (2) 100% O2. (3) Airway assessment — intubate if apnea or severe distress. (4) Blood culture × 1 → antibiotics IMMEDIATELY. (5) NS 20 mL/kg × 2–3 rapid boluses (if tolerating). (6) Dopamine or epinephrine if shock persists after 40 mL/kg. (7) Glucose Q30 min. (8) Transport CALLED.
popup.dosing: Dopamine: 5–10 mcg/kg/min (titrate to 20). Epinephrine: 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min for cold shock. Norepinephrine: 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min for warm/distributive shock. Hydrocortisone: 1–2 mg/kg IV q8h if catecholamine-resistant. Calcium gluconate: 100–200 mg/kg IV over 30 min if iCa <1.0.
popup.evidence: SSC Pediatric 2020: 10–20 mL/kg boluses up to 40–60 mL/kg first hour. Epinephrine or norepinephrine suggested over dopamine as first-line (PMID 32032273). Dopamine no longer recommended as first-line per SSC-Peds.
popup.alerts: TRANSPORT TEAM NOW. Do not delay for culture results. Source control: identify and treat infection source (LP when stable, abdominal imaging, UA).

popup.protocols: Key sources: respiratory (pneumonia → S. pneumoniae), urinary (pyelonephritis → E. coli), CNS (meningitis → N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae), skin/soft tissue (MRSA), abdominal (enteric GNB). Physical exam: identify source. Check meningismus, skin rash (petechiae!), abdominal tenderness, joint swelling.
popup.dosing: Empiric: Ceftriaxone 50–100 mg/kg IV q24h (max 2g) + Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q6h. Adjust if source identified (e.g., add metronidazole if abdominal).
popup.evidence: Weiss & Fitzgerald, Pediatrics 2024. Cruz et al., J ACEP 2020.
popup.alerts: MENINGOCOCCEMIA ALERT: petechiae/purpura + fever = give ceftriaxone IMMEDIATELY. Do NOT delay for LP in unstable child. Notify public health.

popup.protocols: Non-blanching petechiae/purpura in a febrile child = meningococcemia emergency. Press a glass on the rash — if it does NOT blanch (fade) under pressure, it is non-blanching = DIC/microvascular thrombosis = TREAT AS MENINGOCOCCEMIA.
popup.evidence: Meningococcal septicemia: classic purpura fulminans with DIC. Mortality without treatment can reach 40–60% within hours of presentation.
popup.alerts: Even a single petechial lesion above the nipple line in a febrile ill child should be treated as meningococcemia until proven otherwise.

popup.protocols: MENINGOCOCCEMIA EMERGENCY PROTOCOL: (1) Immediate large-bore IV × 2 or IO. (2) Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV (max 2g) STAT — THIS IS THE PRIORITY. (3) 20 mL/kg NS × 2 rapid boluses. (4) Blood cultures × 2. (5) DO NOT PERFORM LP in unstable child. (6) If shock persists: norepinephrine 0.05–0.2 mcg/kg/min. (7) FFP if DIC (Plt <50k, PT >1.5× normal). (8) CALL TRANSPORT NOW. (9) Notify public health — close contact prophylaxis required.
popup.dosing: Ceftriaxone: 50 mg/kg IV (max 2g) q12–24h. Norepinephrine: 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min. FFP: 10–15 mL/kg. Dexamethasone: 0.15 mg/kg q6h × 4 days IF bacterial meningitis suspected AND before or with first antibiotic dose (reduces neurologic sequelae from S. pneumoniae meningitis). Prophylaxis for close contacts: rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone single dose per public health guidance.
popup.evidence: N. meningitidis serogroups B and C most common in USA. Ceftriaxone achieves excellent CSF penetration. Purpura fulminans mortality: 10–40% even with treatment. Public health notification: mandatory reportable disease in all 50 states.
popup.alerts: PURPURA FULMINANS = SKIN NECROSIS FROM DIC. Aggressive FFP + cryoprecipitate + platelets. Limb-threatening. Consider protein C concentrate if available. DO NOT DELAY ANTIBIOTICS FOR ANY REASON.

popup.protocols: Standard Pediatric Septic Shock Protocol: (1) IV × 2. (2) Blood cultures × 1–2 sets. (3) UA/urine culture if tolerated. (4) CXR if respiratory source suspected. (5) Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin IV STAT. (6) 20 mL/kg NS or LR over 15–30 min — up to 40–60 mL/kg first hour. (7) Vasopressors if fluid-refractory. (8) Glucose, iStat Q30–60 min.
popup.dosing: Ceftriaxone: 50–100 mg/kg IV q24h (max 2g). Vancomycin: 15–20 mg/kg IV q6h. Fluid: 20 mL/kg NS or LR boluses. Epinephrine (cold/warm shock): 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min. Norepinephrine (warm/distributive): 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min. Vasopressin (catecholamine-resistant): 0.03–0.06 units/min fixed dose.
popup.evidence: SSC Pediatric 2020: epinephrine/norepinephrine over dopamine for first-line. Balanced crystalloids over NS for large-volume resuscitation. POCUS to guide resuscitation if available.
popup.alerts: REFRACTORY SHOCK: if shock persists after 60 mL/kg + 2 vasopressors, consider: adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone), cardiac tamponade (POCUS), tension pneumothorax, ECMO criteria.

popup.protocols: Assess response after each 20 mL/kg bolus: improving HR? improving CRT? improving mental status? improving lactate? If YES → continue monitoring, repeat lactate, transport. If NO → fluid-refractory shock → vasopressors NOW.
popup.evidence: ACCM 2017: fluid-refractory shock defined as persistent shock after ≥40 mL/kg crystalloid. FEAST trial context: aggressive fluid in resource-limited settings increased mortality — support for careful reassessment after each bolus.
popup.alerts: Do NOT give unlimited fluid without reassessment. Signs of fluid overload: increasing respiratory distress, pulmonary crackles, hepatomegaly, oxygen requirement increase → stop fluids, start vasopressors.

popup.protocols: Continue: (1) Antibiotics running. (2) Serial lactate every 90–120 min — target clearance >10–20%/2h. (3) Glucose Q30–60 min. (4) Transport team en route or called. (5) Re-evaluate for source (LP if stable, UA, blood cultures). (6) Continue antibiotic coverage until cultures return.
popup.evidence: Lactate clearance as resuscitation target: every 10–20% decrease per 2h = adequate response (pediatric ROC analysis).
popup.alerts: Clinical improvement ≠ resolved. Transport is still indicated for all pediatric septic shock. PICU-level monitoring required.

popup.protocols: FLUID-REFRACTORY SHOCK: (1) Start vasopressor IMMEDIATELY via peripheral IV or IO — do NOT wait for central access. (2) Epinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min (cold/cardiogenic) OR Norepinephrine 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min (warm/distributive). (3) Consider hydrocortisone if catecholamine-resistant. (4) POCUS if available — assess cardiac function, rule out tamponade. (5) TRANSPORT — PICU mandatory. (6) Consider intubation if work of breathing is impaired.
popup.dosing: Epinephrine: 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min peripheral IV/IO. Norepinephrine: 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min. Vasopressin (add-on): 0.03–0.06 units/min fixed dose. Hydrocortisone: 1–2 mg/kg IV q6–8h stress dose. Dopamine (if epi/NE not available): 5–20 mcg/kg/min.
popup.evidence: SSC Pediatric 2020: epinephrine/norepinephrine first-line over dopamine. Peripheral vasopressor administration acceptable when no central access. NeoCardioLab 2024–2025: hemodynamic phenotyping guides vasopressor selection.
popup.alerts: ECMO CONSIDERATION: refractory septic shock unresponsive to ≥2 vasopressors at maximum doses + >100 mL/kg fluid is a potential ECMO candidate. Transfer to ECMO-capable center urgently. Discuss with receiving PICU immediately.

popup.protocols: Adolescent septic shock approaches adult Sepsis-3 criteria: persistent hypotension (MAP <65) despite fluids + vasopressors + lactate >2 mmol/L. Organisms: N. meningitidis, S. aureus (MRSA), S. pneumoniae, enteric GNB. Additional considerations: toxic shock syndrome (TSA/Group A Strep), necrotizing fasciitis, sexually acquired (PID, gonorrhea), substance use.
popup.dosing: Empiric: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12–24h + Vancomycin 25–30 mg/kg/day ÷ q6h (AUC/MIC target 400–600). Add metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h if abdominal source. Fluid: 30 mL/kg NS or LR within 3h (adult Sepsis-3 bundle). Vasopressor: norepinephrine 0.01–3 mcg/kg/min (first-line adult/adolescent).
popup.evidence: Singer et al., JAMA 2016 (Sepsis-3): adult septic shock definition. SSC adult guidelines. Consider age-appropriate Sepsis-3 criteria for adolescents ≥14 years.
popup.alerts: TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME: diffuse erythroderma + fever + hypotension + multi-organ failure. Clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV q8h (inhibits toxin production) + anti-staphylococcal coverage. IVIG considered for severe cases.

popup.protocols: ADOLESCENT PROTOCOL: (1) Large-bore IV × 2. (2) Blood cultures × 2 sets. (3) Ceftriaxone 2g + Vancomycin IV STAT. (4) 30 mL/kg NS or LR over 30–60 min. (5) Reassess: if MAP <65 after fluids → norepinephrine. (6) Monitor: lactate, UO (target >0.5 mL/kg/h), MAP (target ≥65). (7) Source control: LP (if stable), CXR, CT abdomen/pelvis if abdominal source, wound/abscess drainage. (8) PICU transfer.
popup.dosing: Norepinephrine: 0.01–3 mcg/kg/min (first-line). Vasopressin: 0.03 units/min add-on. Hydrocortisone: 50 mg IV q6h (stress dose) if catecholamine-refractory. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h × 4 days if bacterial meningitis. PRBC: if Hgb <7 g/dL or <10 with cardiac compromise.
popup.evidence: SSC Adult/Adolescent 2021. Weiss & Fitzgerald Pediatrics 2024.
popup.alerts: NECROTIZING FASCIITIS: severe pain, wooden-hard tissue, rapid spread despite antibiotics → SURGICAL EMERGENCY. CT imaging + immediate OR. Add clindamycin for Group A Strep toxin inhibition. Mortality 25–35% even with surgery.

content.heading: The Inflammatory Cascade
content.text: When bacteria enter the bloodstream, their structural components (PAMPs) bind host immune receptors. Gram-negative LPS binds TLR-4 → massive TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 release → nitric oxide synthase activation → profound vasodilation → distributive shock. Gram-positive LTA/peptidoglycan binds TLR-2; superantigens (TSST-1, SPE) bypass normal antigen presentation → activate 5–30% of T-cells directly → cytokine storm.

content.heading: Warm vs. Cold Shock
content.text: Warm shock: high CO, low SVR, bounding pulses, flash CRT, fever — more common in older children with GNB sepsis. Cold shock: low CO, high SVR, weak pulses, mottling, prolonged CRT — DOMINANT PATTERN IN NEONATES due to immature myocardial reserve. Management differs: warm shock → vasopressors (norepinephrine); cold shock → inotropes (dopamine, epinephrine).

content.heading: Why Neonates Differ
content.text: The neonatal myocardium has reduced calcium stores, fewer mitochondria, and less contractile reserve. Very preterm neonates have relative adrenal insufficiency, low baseline SVR (partially maintained by PDA physiology), and a brain at high risk for IVH from rapid hemodynamic changes. These factors make volume resuscitation more dangerous in preterm neonates and hydrocortisone more commonly needed.

content.heading: EOS Organisms (< 72h)
content.text: GRAM-POSITIVE: Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae) — most common USA EOS cause; Listeria monocytogenes — rare but requires ampicillin (NOT cephalosporins). GRAM-NEGATIVE: Escherichia coli — increasing incidence, especially in preterm; Klebsiella pneumoniae. Coverage: Ampicillin + Gentamicin covers all four.

content.heading: LOS Organisms (≥ 72h)
content.text: GRAM-POSITIVE: CoNS (S. epidermidis) — most common NICU pathogen, indolent, central-line associated; MRSA — aggressive, toxin-mediated, line-associated. GRAM-NEGATIVE: Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter — NEC-associated, resistant patterns possible. Coverage: Vancomycin + Gentamicin; add Pip-Tazo or Cefepime if Pseudomonas risk.

content.heading: Mortality Pattern
content.text: Gram-negative organisms account for 70% of neonatal septic shock cases and 90% of fatal cases (Gago 2022). In the USA, CoNS is the most common LOS pathogen but has the lowest mortality. MRSA LOS carries higher mortality than MSSA. Gram-negative LOS produces the most explosive hemodynamic collapse via endotoxin-mediated mechanisms.

content.heading: Lactic Acid
content.text: Normal: <2 mmol/L. Tissue hypoperfusion → anaerobic glycolysis → lactate accumulation. Lactate 2–4: significant hypoperfusion, treat aggressively. Lactate >4: critical — 22× higher mortality risk vs <1 (pediatric ROC analysis). Target: >10–20% clearance per 2-hour resuscitation interval. Lactate clearance = [(initial – current) / initial] × 100.

content.heading: Base Deficit
content.text: Normal: –2 to +2 mEq/L. Reflects integrated metabolic acidosis severity. BD –2 to –5: mild. BD –5 to –10: moderate, aggressive treatment needed. BD –10 to –15: severe, vasopressors + transport now. BD < –15: critical, near-fatal acidosis. Neonatal Wynn-Wong criterion: BD >5 contributes to septic shock diagnosis.

content.heading: Anion Gap
content.text: Formula: Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Normal 8–12 mEq/L. In septic shock: elevated AG = lactic acidosis. Albumin correction: corrected AG = measured AG + 2.5 × (4 – albumin g/dL). CRITICAL IN NEONATES: always consider inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) in elevated AG. Organic acidemias (propionic, methylmalonic), urea cycle defects, MSUD, GA1 mimic septic shock — always send ammonia in neonates with unexplained elevated AG.

content.heading: Procalcitonin (PCT)
content.text: PCT >10 ng/mL: strongly suggests gram-negative bacteremia. Normal: <0.5 ng/mL. PCT peaks at 24–48h after infection onset. Useful for distinguishing bacterial (high PCT) from viral infection (low/normal PCT). Not available point-of-care in most rural settings — use clinical judgment and CRP trend when PCT unavailable.

content.heading: Dopamine
content.text: Dose: 5–20 mcg/kg/min. Low (1–3): dopaminergic — renal/mesenteric vasodilation. Mid (5–15): beta-1 inotrope + alpha vasopressor. High (>15): predominantly alpha vasoconstriction. First-line for neonates historically (92% of NICU septic shock cases, Foote 2023). Can be given peripherally. Hydrocortisone adjuvant significantly reduces mortality in neonatal septic shock (aOR 0.60).

content.heading: Epinephrine (Adrenaline)
content.text: Dose: 0.05–1 mcg/kg/min. Low (<0.1): beta-dominant (inotrope + vasodilator). High (>0.3): alpha-dominant vasoconstriction. Use for cold shock with cardiac failure. SSC-Peds 2020 suggests as first-line over dopamine. However, Foote 2023 showed epinephrine ALONE associated with higher neonatal mortality (aOR 4.7) vs dopamine alone. Clinical judgment required.

content.heading: Norepinephrine
content.text: Dose: 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min. Potent alpha vasoconstriction + moderate beta-1 inotropy. First-line for warm/distributive shock in older children and adolescents (SSC-Peds recommended). Less evidence in neonates. Requires more cardiac reserve than epinephrine for cold shock pattern.

content.heading: Hydrocortisone
content.text: Stress dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV q6–8h (neonate/child). 50 mg IV q6h (adolescent). Indication: catecholamine-resistant shock; suspected relative adrenal insufficiency (common in premature neonates, prolonged ICU stay). Evidence: Foote 2023 multicenter — hydrocortisone adjuvant aOR 0.60 for mortality in neonatal septic shock. Do NOT use routine prophylactic steroids.

content.heading: When to Call
content.text: Call transport at the MOMENT of recognition — not after stabilization. Indications: any suspected septic shock (any age); lactate >4 mmol/L; BD < –10; vasopressor-dependent shock; DIC; respiratory failure; petechiae/purpura; neonate <72h with any signs of illness; altered mental status/seizures. It is always easier to cancel a transport than to wait too long.

content.heading: Pre-Transport Priorities
content.text: (1) Secure IV/IO access. (2) Antibiotics given and documented. (3) Fluid resuscitation initiated. (4) Vasopressor running if needed. (5) Glucose corrected. (6) Airway secured if respiratory compromise (intubate BEFORE transport if possible). (7) Temperature stabilized. (8) SBAR call completed with receiving NICU/PICU.

content.heading: SBAR Template
content.text: SITUATION: [age/sex] with suspected septic shock requiring urgent transfer. BACKGROUND: gestational age, maternal history (neonates), onset, prior antibiotics, PMH. ASSESSMENT: vital signs, blood gas values (pH, BD, lactate, AG), labs, antibiotics given and time. RECOMMENDATION: requesting emergent transport; vasopressor dose; ventilation status; specific questions for receiving team.
